surfaces.source: https://code.claude.com/docs/en/skills; path literal read from the 2.1.251 artifact
surfaces.note:
Two neighbouring products read this directory, measured from their own pinned bytes. Grok's embedded reference: `skills = true  # scan ~/.claude/skills/ and <cwd>/.claude/skills/`, User tier, Lowest priority, configurable. OpenCode carries `.claude/skills/<name>/SKILL.md` as a path literal and the vendor lists it as *Global Claude-compatible*. This provider's ownership is unchanged -- it is Claude Code's own home and this is the harness this provider configures -- but a namespace is removed whole, so a remove here also changes what Grok and OpenCode see. `remove` says the namespaces go whole; it cannot say who else was reading them. Confirmed 2026-08-29 from the 2.1.251 artifact, whose bytes match this baseline's own sha256: the product carries `.claude/skills` as a literal, 51 time(s), joined to the home its `CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR` resolves. The vendor page beside it says the same thing; what the artifact adds is that a wrong path here would now be visible to something rather than to nobody.

**Two kinds, and the product distinguishes them by manifest.** Its own reference: *"Any folder under a skills directory that contains a `.claude-plugin/plugin.json` manifest is loaded as a plugin named `<name>@skills-dir` on the next session, with no marketplace and no install step."* Its table gives all three shapes: `<skills-dir>/foo/SKILL.md` with no manifest is a skill `foo`; `<skills-dir>/foo/.claude-plugin/plugin.json` is a plugin `foo@skills-dir` that can bundle its own skills, agents and hooks; `<plugin>/skills/bar/SKILL.md` is a skill packaged inside a plugin. The scope table names `~/.claude/skills/` as **personal**, loading *in every project*, with the workspace trust gate applying only to the project-scope directory.

`plugin` was undeclared here until 2026-08-29 on the reasoning that a plugin projects through `settings.json` -- true of *enabling* one, and never the whole question. This mechanism needs no settings key, no marketplace and no install.

surfaces.note:
"Personal rules in ~/.claude/rules/ apply to every project on your machine." Markdown files, optionally with a `paths` frontmatter list that scopes a rule to matching files. Owned so a setup can carry one; no component kind routes here, because `instruction` already routes to CLAUDE.md and one kind with two surfaces would leave a compiler to choose with nothing telling it how Confirmed 2026-08-29 from the 2.1.251 artifact, whose bytes match this baseline's own sha256: the product carries `.claude/rules` as a literal, 9 time(s), joined to the home its `CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR` resolves. **Written down 2026-08-30 rather than left implying it is coming, and the consumer's measurement makes the reason stronger than this row put it.** This said one kind on two surfaces leaves a compiler choosing with nothing telling it how. The consumer measured its own lookup: `rule_for(component_type, harness_id)` scans its rule table and returns the **first** match. So a second row for one kind is not ambiguous-and-unresolved -- it is *unreachable, silently*. Nothing would refuse it and nothing would say it was skipped.

The inverse already works and is in that table: claude's `plugin` and `skill` both project to `skills` -- two kinds sharing one path, two lookups, no collision. One kind on two paths is the direction the lookup cannot express.

**And this is not waiting on a release.** Per-surface selection is not on the consumer's roadmap, and if it arrives it changes the component model rather than the table: a component would have to name its surface, which is a passport field and an architecture decision. So there is no consumer version to re-ask this against. Re-ask when a passport carries a surface name; the consumer will say when one does.

Personal workflow scripts. The vendor: a script saved to `~/.claude/workflows/` is *just for you*, in contrast to a `.claude/workflows/` shared in a repository, and it *runs as a `/<name>` command*. The binary carries `.claude/workflows/` without a `~`, which is why the root took a page to settle -- the audit had called it global on the strength of the literal alone and was corrected before anything was built on it.

Owned from 2026-08-28 so a backup captures it. **Routing no kind**, for the reason grok's `rules` row gives: `command` already routes to the owned `commands`, and one kind on two surfaces makes a consumer's route ambiguous -- the surfaces guard refuses it by name. Both are real, both are user-level, and which a `command` component should reach waits on the per-kind route the consumer is building.

There is no .mcp.json under this home. `.claude.json` is in never_touch, so no MCP surface is ownable inside this target and the kind is not declared.

Hooks are configured under a "hooks" key in settings.json. ~/.claude/hooks/ is a convention for the scripts a hook command points at, not a directory Claude Code reads. It is declared the day a setup here ships hook scripts and not before.

Claude Code owns plugins/known_marketplaces.json, plugins/marketplaces, plugins/cache and plugins/data -- the state a marketplace install copies into. Held in never_touch for that reason, and it is product state rather than a surface a provider writes.

**This is no longer the reason the `plugin` kind is undeclared, because it is declared.** The old text ended *a plugin component projects through settings.json, which this provider does own* -- true of enabling a plugin, and it hid a second mechanism entirely. declined.reason:
Not a path in the target, and named without an extension for that reason: `managed-settings.json` lives at a **system** path, one per operating system, and every recorded path here is relative to the target.

  * Linux — `/etc/claude-code/managed-settings.json`
  * macOS — `/Library/Application Support/ClaudeCode/managed-settings.json`
  * Windows — the `HKLM SOFTWARE/Policies/ClaudeCode` registry key, and `C:/Program Files/ClaudeCode/managed-settings.json`

**The Windows line was `%ProgramData%\\ClaudeCode\\managed-settings.json` until 2026-08-30, and the sentence beside all three said they were path literals in the pinned product. Re-measured at 2.1.251, none of the three is.** Asked of both shipped artifacts -- `claude-code-linux-x64` and `claude-code-win32-x64`, each digest-checked against this baseline's own table before extracting:

```
                                                        win  linux
  /etc/claude-code/managed-settings.json                  0     0
  /Library/Application Support/ClaudeCode/managed-...     0     0
  ProgramData\\ClaudeCode\\managed-settings.json          0     0
  Program Files/ClaudeCode/managed-settings.json          1     1
  SOFTWARE/Policies/ClaudeCode                            1     1
  /etc/nddev-invented/managed-settings.json               0     0   (control)
  NddevInvented/ClaudeCode/managed-settings.json          0     0   (control)
```

The controls return zero, so the search discriminates. The three per-OS paths are joined at runtime -- the bytes carry `f(r,"managed-settings.json")` and `zt(iR,"managed-settings.json")` rather than any assembled form -- which is why every runtime-joined path in this record reads `page` and why a literal search cannot confirm one. **What the bytes do carry is one sentence naming the Windows pair**, and it is the only place in either artifact where a managed-settings path appears assembled:

> *"the HKLM SOFTWARE/Policies/ClaudeCode registry key or C:/Program Files/ClaudeCode/managed-settings.json — WSL reads managed settings from the full Windows policy chain (HKLM, C:/Program Files/ClaudeCode via DrvFs, HKCU)"*

So the old Windows value was wrong and its replacement is measured rather than read off a page. `ProgramData` does occur in these bytes, four times, and none is about this product's policy: a sandbox base-named-objects list, a trust-CA helper, and an Azure agent token path. A grep that stopped at the bare word would have confirmed the wrong answer.

**And one thing neither the old record nor the review had.** That sentence documents `wslInheritsWindowsSettings`: with it set in an admin-only Windows source, a WSL process reads the **Windows** policy chain rather than the Linux one. WSL is therefore not simply a Linux host for this product's policy layer, and a record that treats it as one answers the wrong question for a machine where that switch is on. Grok's own compatibility documentation describes the file, and the description is the reason this row exists: *"a protected policy file for allowlists and defaults. Its values take precedence over user, project and local config **and cannot be overridden**."*

**It bears on the `full-auto` posture.** That setup writes `permissions.defaultMode = bypassPermissions` and `sandbox.enabled = false` into the owned `settings.json`. Under a managed policy those keys are correct, at a correct path, in a file the product reads — and a higher layer overrides them. The setup installs, verifies and restores cleanly and **changes nothing**.

That is the third instance of one defect class in this estate: opencode's bare-string `permission`, antigravity's `toolPermissions`, and now a correct key under a layer that outranks it. The first two were fixed by writing the right key; this one cannot be fixed by writing anything, which is why it is written down instead.

**Nothing to own and nothing to check at runtime.** A provider that read a system policy in order to warn about it would be reading a file it promises not to touch, on a path outside every target it is given.

A negative is worth what its control is worth, and here the control is another vendor answering yes to the identical question.

permission_boundary.note:
**What `permissions.deny` bounds, and what it does not.** The `baseline` posture writes `Read(./.env)` and `Read(./.env.*)`, and a reader can take that for a secrets boundary. It is not one, and the product says so in its own shipped bytes rather than only on a page.

Two mechanisms, and they are not the same boundary:

* `permissions.deny` is **per tool**. The artifact's own prompt text reads *"Each rule names a tool and (optionally) an argument pattern that is already hard-blocked for that"* tool, and elsewhere warns the model against *"`python -c`, `sed -i`, `cat >`, heredocs, or similar to write or edit a file that an Edit/Write/MultiEdit deny rule covers, or otherwise routing around a deny rule by switching tools"*. That sentence is instruction to a model, not enforcement: it exists because the other route is open.
* `sandbox` carries a separate `denyReadPaths`, and the Linux implementation works by mounting over the path -- the bytes log *"Re-bound write path wiped by denyRead tmpfs"* and *"Re-applying denyRead tmpfs re-exposed by denyWrite bind"*. That is a filesystem boundary and it applies to whatever runs inside the sandbox, not only to one tool.

Searched with a control: an invented mechanism name is absent from the same bytes, so the readings above are not a search that matches anything.

**Recorded rather than acted on.** Adding a sandbox deny path to `baseline` would change what that posture means, and a posture is a promise somebody already selected. What was wrong was the description calling it *a conservative permission rule* and stopping, which leaves a reader to supply the stronger meaning themselves.

libc_coverage.note:
**The vendor ships musl builds and this table pins none.** Read from the registry's own `optionalDependencies` for 2.1.251 rather than from a page: eight platform packages, of which `linux-x64-musl` and `linux-arm64-musl` have no row here. On a musl system `artifact_for("linux", "x86_64")` answers with the glibc build, which is a false statement about capability.

**How far it actually reaches is narrower than that, and the measurement is the reason.** This provider's own released binary is glibc-linked: the 0.0.40 asset `claude-setup-system-x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu` reads as *dynamically linked, interpreter `/lib64/ld-linux-x86-64.so.2`*, `NEEDED libc.so.6`, and there is no musl asset. So on Alpine this program does not start, and nobody can reach the wrong answer through it. The path that reaches it is a provider built from source against a musl target -- then it runs, and then it hands back a product artifact that will not.

**Which fixes the order.** Adding musl rows to this table alone would publish an answer nobody can ask for. A musl provider build has to come with them, or before them.

**And there is nowhere in the contract to say it.** Measured by the consumer at this protocol version: `provider-info.schema.json` requires `supported_os` and `supported_arch` and carries no libc anywhere. Both are open arrays of free strings, so a spelling like `linux-musl` would *validate* and still not work -- the consumer builds its match key as `f"{os}/{arch}"` and splits on exactly one `/`, and there is no third axis to split into. So no spelling is invented here. This is a v3 vocabulary extension when it comes, and until it does the honest state is a recorded gap rather than a platform string nobody parses.

source_verified_runtime_flags_note:
Read out of the 2.1.251 artifact on 2026-08-31, after its digest was checked against the artifact table: `DISABLE_UPDATES` nine times, `DISABLE_AUTOUPDATER` eleven, `DISABLE_UPGRADE_COMMAND` four, and an invented name zero, so the search discriminates.

**This block did not exist until now, and launch has set `DISABLE_UPDATES` since 0.0.42.** The measurement was written in the declaration's own comment, which is a claim about method with the method a git archaeology away -- the same defect as a total without its root. `the_switch_it_sets_was_measured` reads this list for every harness that forces a switch, and it caught this one the first time it ran.

`DISABLE_UPDATES` is the one set, because the vendor documents it as stopping manual updates too: an autoupdater switched off still leaves `claude update` able to replace the bytes this provider pinned.

surface_presence.method: Every namespace this harness declares, global and scoped, searched as a fixed string in the artifact the current pin names, digest verified before reading; both the declared path and its last segment counted, because a product that composes a path by joining segments never spells the whole of it. A count here is a lower bound and not a routing proof -- what it answers is whether a surface vanished from the product under a version bump, which five of the seven took on 2026-09-02. The invented control was searched in the same run and found nowhere, so the search discriminates.
